questions.prompt: Which update is eligible for PostgreSQL's HOT optimization?

options.label: It changes only columns not referenced by regular indexes, and the new tuple fits on the same heap page.
It changes a unique-index key but leaves the primary key unchanged.
It changes only unindexed columns, but the new tuple must move to another heap page.

questions.explanation: HOT requires both index eligibility and enough space for the successor tuple on the original heap page. It remains an internal per-row decision.

questions.prompt: Fill the physical-location requirement for a HOT successor tuple.
questions.template: The new row version must fit on the {{blank}} as the old row version.
questions.explanation: The existing index entry can lead through the HOT chain because every version stays on the original heap page.

questions.prompt: Order the lifecycle of a repeated HOT-updated row.

items.label: An index entry reaches the root page item
PostgreSQL follows same-page tuple links for the visible version
Page pruning removes intermediate versions no snapshot needs
Freed page items and space become reusable

questions.explanation: One index entry can continue to reach a same-page version chain while pruning removes versions that have become globally invisible.

questions.prompt: Match each index dependency to its HOT consequence.
questions.explanation: INCLUDE, expression, and partial-predicate dependencies block HOT. PostgreSQL 16 added the BRIN summarizing-index exception.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate review of lowering table fillfactor from 100 to 80?

options.label: It reserves future same-page update room but increases the heap footprint and does not immediately repack existing pages.
It guarantees that every update will be HOT, including indexed-column updates.
It only changes B-tree page density and has no effect on heap pages.

questions.explanation: Lower table fillfactor can improve same-page capacity, but it costs storage and read density. Existing pages are not reorganized merely by changing the setting.

questions.prompt: Which production conclusion is justified by a high n_tup_hot_upd ratio?

options.label: Eligible updates often avoid new regular-index entries, but vacuum health, dead tuples, read indexes, and interval trends still need review.
Autovacuum can be disabled because page pruning now handles every cleanup responsibility.
All indexes on the table should be removed until the HOT ratio reaches 100 percent.

questions.explanation: HOT is one workload signal. It does not replace vacuuming, visibility-map maintenance, transaction-ID freezing, or indexes that justify their read benefit.
